opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that reinforcement learning, at least the way we'd like it to work in the real world, is fundamentally about improving on something you can already do somewhat. If you drop a robot into the world with a randomly initialized policy and ask it to learn to fold laundry from trial and error, it's just never going to get there. The space of possible behaviors is enormous, and the chance of stumbling onto something that gets any reward signal at all is basically zero.

So what supervised learning gives you, whether that's imitation learning from human demonstrations or pretraining on large amounts of robot and web data, is a starting point. It puts the policy into the right neighborhood. The robot already knows roughly what a shirt is, roughly how to grasp it, roughly what folding looks like. And then reinforcement learning can do what it's actually good at, which is refining that behavior, making it more robust, figuring out how to recover from mistakes, getting faster and more reliable than the demonstrations it started from.

There's a nice analogy with language models here. The big leaps we've seen from RL on language models happened because there was a really strong pretrained model underneath. RL didn't teach the model language; it took a model that already had a lot of knowledge and sharpened how it uses that knowledge. I think robotics is going to follow a very similar pattern. Supervised learning on diverse data builds the prior, and RL turns that prior into real competence.

And the other piece I'd add is that supervised learning is just much more stable and scalable as a training procedure. It's easy to throw a lot of data and compute at it and get predictable improvements. RL is more finicky. So it makes sense to do as much of the heavy lifting as you can with the stable tool, and then use RL for that last stretch where you actually need the system to learn from its own experience and go beyond what any demonstrator showed it. That's where I think the really exciting stuff happens, but you need that foundation to get there.

r001.rationale: The response says supervised learning gives the policy a useful starting point so RL can refine it and learn from its own experience, contrasting this with the near-impossibility of learning from a random policy.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes supervised learning as building a prior or starting point that RL then turns into more robust competence.

r003.rationale: It predicts that robotics will follow the LLM pattern: supervised learning builds the prior, and RL then improves how that prior is used.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing to understand is that reinforcement learning, in its purest form, is asking a lot. You're asking a system to figure out, entirely from trial and error, both what the world looks like and what it should do in it. And in robotics specifically, trial and error is expensive. Every sample costs you real time, real hardware, sometimes a broken gripper. So the question I keep coming back to is: what can we get for free, or nearly for free, before we start paying that price?

And the answer is that a huge amount of what a robot needs to know isn't really about decision-making at all. It's about perception, about understanding that this is a cup and that's a table and the cup is on the table. It's about having a prior over what reasonable motions look like. Supervised learning, whether that's imitation from demonstrations or large-scale pretraining on video and language, is incredibly good at absorbing that kind of structure. It's data-efficient in the sense that matters: the data already exists, or it's cheap to collect, and the learning signal is dense.

So what supervised learning gives you is a starting point that's already in the right neighborhood. The policy already does something sensible. The representation already carves the world up in roughly the right way. And then RL becomes the thing it's actually good at, which is refinement. Fixing the last ten percent. Learning the parts of the task that no demonstrator did quite right, or adapting to a situation that wasn't in the data. That's a much smaller search problem than starting from random weights.

I also think there's a deeper point, which is that in robotics the bottleneck has never really been the algorithm. It's been generalization. A policy that works in one lab and falls apart in another is useless. And the field that has actually solved generalization, at scale, is supervised learning on enormous datasets. Language models are the obvious example. So if you want robot learning to inherit that property, you want its foundation to be built the same way, and then you want RL to sit on top as the mechanism for grounding that broad knowledge in actual physical consequences.

So I don't see it as supervised versus reinforcement learning. I see supervised learning as the thing that makes RL tractable at all in the real world.

r001.rationale: The candidate says supervised learning gives the policy and representation a useful starting point, making RL a smaller search problem focused on refinement.

r002.rationale: It describes supervised learning as supplying structure and broad knowledge before RL grounds and refines that knowledge through physical experience.

r003.rationale: The candidate uses LLMs as an example of generalization and argues robotics should be built similarly, but does not predict that foundation-model development generally will follow an LLM-like supervised-pretraining-then-RL trajectory.

astra-6.text:
Well, supervised learning gives us a way to learn a lot of the structure of a problem before we ask the system to figure out how to solve it through trial and error. In robotics, that matters because collecting experience is expensive. You have to run a physical robot, things take time, things break, and you can’t necessarily afford millions of attempts starting from random behavior.

If you have demonstrations, you can use supervised learning to train a policy to imitate those demonstrations. That gives you a starting point where the robot already does something reasonably sensible. Reinforcement learning can then improve that behavior based on whether it actually succeeds.

But there’s also a deeper connection. A lot of what happens inside a reinforcement learning algorithm is supervised learning. You’re fitting a value function to targets, or training a policy to produce actions that you’ve estimated are good. The difficult additional piece is that your data depends on your own behavior, and the targets themselves can change as you learn.

So I think of supervised learning as providing both the machinery and a useful initialization. The limitation of imitation alone is that you’re learning to reproduce what somebody did, rather than learning directly from the consequences of your actions. If the robot makes a mistake and ends up somewhere the demonstrator never went, it may not know how to recover. Reinforcement learning gives it a way to learn from that experience—and, potentially, to become better than the demonstrations it started with.

r001.rationale: The response says supervised learning lets the robot learn problem structure before trial and error and gives it a sensible starting point, so reinforcement learning can build on its own experience.

r002.rationale: It describes using demonstrations for supervised imitation to initialize a robot policy, which reinforcement learning can then improve.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss the general development trajectory of foundation models or compare it with LLM training.

sol-6.1.text:
Supervised learning gives us a way to learn useful representations and behaviors from data before we ask a robot to improve through interaction. If you have demonstrations, you can train a policy to predict the actions a person would take. That can get you to a reasonable starting point without requiring the robot to discover everything through trial and error.

But predicting actions has a limitation: the robot’s actions affect what it sees next. If it makes a small mistake, it might end up in a situation that wasn’t represented in the demonstrations, and then the mistakes can compound. Reinforcement learning lets us optimize for the consequences of those actions—whether the robot actually completes the task—and potentially learn to recover when things go wrong.

So I see them as complementary. Supervised learning lets us absorb prior experience efficiently, and reinforcement learning provides a mechanism for improving that behavior based on what actually happens when you execute it.

r001.rationale: It says supervised learning gives the robot a useful starting point and lets it absorb prior experience efficiently before improving through interaction.

r002.rationale: It presents supervised learning as a way to supply prior experience first, then reinforcement learning as a way to improve behavior based on execution.

r003.rationale: It does not predict a general foundation-model trajectory modeled on LLMs, or mention that sequence as a trend.
